lines: Every example run so far in this chapter has quietly assumed one setting was already on.
Here's what that setting actually is, and what changed the moment it flipped.
That setting flips the answer to a simple question: what happens when a calculation goes wrong.
An overflow, a value that can't be converted, a split by nothing at all -- each of those used to come back as nothing, silently. Now each one stops the query and says so.
Here's a question worth sitting with before the answer comes.

Take the largest whole number a thirty-two bit slot can hold, and add one more to it, with the new setting on. Does that raise an error, or does it quietly wrap around to a negative number the way it used to?
steps.answer: It raises an error. Wrapping silently to a negative number is exactly the behavior this setting turns off.

lines: Raises an error, and that's measured directly, not assumed.
Turn the new setting off, and the identical calculation goes back to wrapping around to a negative number -- the old behavior, still there underneath.
There's a second place this same idea shows up, and it's worth separating from the first.
Converting a value on its way into a table follows its own, separate rule -- one that can be dialed independently of the main setting this topic is about.
Here's a second question, same shape as the first.
Take a letter that can't possibly be a number, and try to convert it to a whole number, with the new setting on. Does that raise an error, or does it quietly come back empty?
steps.answer: It raises an error. A conversion that can't work is now treated the same way an overflow is.

lines: Raises an error here too, and again, measured directly.
With the setting off, that same impossible conversion comes back empty instead -- matching what it did before the setting existed.
There's a deliberate escape hatch, and it's worth knowing it exists.
A handful of functions, each one a forgiving version of an ordinary operation, come back empty on purpose instead of raising -- one expression opting out, without switching the whole setting off.
Carrying an older job forward onto this version has a method, and it's a mechanical one.
Run the same set of checks under the old behavior and the new one, compare every difference in the output, and look closely at each conversion that difference points to.
One setting, flipped, changed what a wrong calculation does by default -- from quietly nothing, to a stop and a reason why.
And a small, named set of exceptions exists for exactly the cases where quietly nothing is still what's wanted.
